claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins in a high-temperature, disordered BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and chemical driving forces for local ordering.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the alloy's disordered high-temperature BCC phase.
Chemical driving forces involving Al become dominant as temperature decreases.
Loss of entropic stabilization during cooling permits Al partitioning and ordering.
Al-mediated ordering promotes nucleation of secondary phases.
Local chemical ordering involving Al acts as a precursor to ordered secondary or intermetallic phases.
Decreasing the entropic contribution lowers the barrier for chemical ordering.
Diffusion kinetics and local chemical interactions, particularly Al's tendency to order, determine the extent and type of phase transformation.
The interplay between entropy loss and ordering kinetics sets the alloy's phase-transformation pathway.
Slow cooling or intermediate-temperature annealing will produce more ordering than rapid quenching.
Thermally treated samples will show additional or shifted diffraction peaks and local chemical segregation, especially Al-rich regions.
Immediate quenching from the high-temperature BCC state will retain a disordered BCC structure without detectable ordering or secondary phases.
The proposed mechanism applies only where diffusion is active but extensive coarsening or alternative kinetic pathways do not dominate.
Identical samples should be compared after immediate quenching, controlled slow cooling, and isothermal annealing below the high-temperature phase regime.
Failure of every thermal treatment to produce detectable ordering, secondary phases, or Al segregation relative to the quenched control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
